name: Out-group favouritism
statement: Members of low-status groups sometimes evaluate a higher-status outgroup more warmly than their own, and it shows on timed measures rather than questionnaires.
meaning: This is the counter-case to in-group favouritism, and it is narrower than the name suggests. Jost, Banaji and Nosek define it as an evaluative preference for members of a group one does not belong to. Their argument is not that people are motivated to favour outsiders because they are outsiders. It is that members of disadvantaged groups absorb the hierarchy they live in, and the absorption shows up where self-report does not reach. So the claim has two parts, and they come apart. The first is a dissociation: low-status groups say they prefer their own group and score near zero or below on reaction-time measures. The second is that this happens across disadvantaged groups in general. The evidence supports the first in some domains and does not support the second. Almost everything on this page rests on the Implicit-Association Test, which has its own entry here and its own problems.

origin.who: John T. Jost and Mahzarin R. Banaji
origin.note: Their paper proposed system justification partly to account for the prevalence of outgroup favouritism among low-status groups, which they argued social identity theory handled badly. The term is older than the theory. Jost, Banaji and Nosek's own count of index entries in 11 books on intergroup relations published between 1981 and 2000 found 142 for ingroup favouritism and 12 for outgroup favouritism, 8 of the 12 in a single chapter by Hinkle and Brown. The 1994 text was not retrieved for this entry, and the account of it here is the 2004 review's.

evidence: Nosek, Banaji and Greenwald harvested over 600,000 tasks from a demonstration website between October 1998 and April 2000. On the race task using faces, White respondents showed an implicit preference for White over Black at d = 0.83, n = 103,316. Black respondents showed d = 0.16 in the same direction, n = 17,510. The self-reports ran the other way: White respondents preferred White at d = 0.59, Black respondents preferred Black at d = 0.80. Their table by ethnicity gives the face task as 0.83 for White respondents, 0.78 for Asian, 0.66 for Hispanic and 0.16 for Black, and the name task as 1.04, 0.91, 0.88 and 0.28. Age was the flatter and larger effect. On the age face task every ethnic group scored between 0.96 and 1.10 for young over old. Jost, Banaji and Nosek collected three further comparisons from a public site between 2001 and 2003 and reported them in the same units, with positive values meaning ingroup favouritism. White respondents scored 1.06 implicitly, n = 15,229, and Black respondents 0.04, n = 2,011, while explicitly Black respondents scored 0.79 and White respondents 0.62. Respondents aged over 50 scored -0.87 implicitly, n = 815, against 0.99 for the young, n = 12,610. Gay and lesbian respondents scored 0.11 implicitly, n = 3,354, against 1.10 for straight respondents, n = 14,619. The same review reports Rudman, Feinberg and Fairchild's status ranking, in which the widest status gaps carried the strongest reversals: rich 1.73 against poor -1.14, and slim 0.78 against overweight -0.34. Narrower gaps left both sides favouring their own group, white 0.92 against Asian 0.27 and Christian 1.22 against Jewish 0.41.

replication.headline: Implicit preference for the young holds into people's sixties across 49,014 participants, and the race version reverses when all four racial groups are compared in one task.
replication.detail: Axt, Ebersole and Nosek ran three studies with more than 200,000 participants using a four-category variant of the test, which scores each group against the average of the others rather than against one rival. Study 1 drew 97,641 participants between 5 June 2012 and 11 April 2013, of whom 37,314 were classified White, 4,514 Black and 1,756 East Asian. Every racial group placed its own group first, followed by White, Asian, Black and Hispanic, with all pairwise t values above 4.06, all p below .001 and an average d of .2. The single exception was the Black against Hispanic comparison among Asian participants, t(1468) = 0.86, p = .394. Their supplementary table gives Black participants a White-versus-Black score of -0.19, n = 3,728, an Asian-versus-Black score of -0.22 and a Black-versus-Hispanic score of 0.26, all of them favouring the ingroup. Religion behaved the same way. Age did not. Study 3 drew 49,014 participants between 21 April 2011 and 19 January 2012. Every decade band from teens to sixties ranked children above young adults above middle-aged adults above old adults, all t above 2.4, all p below .02, average d = .27. Among the 1,020 participants in their sixties, children scored 0.21 above old adults, young adults 0.09 above and middle-aged adults 0.10 above. The authors write that ingroup identity was swamped by the general pattern of younger is better. Chopik and Giasson pooled 704,151 Project Implicit respondents aged 15 to 94, tested between December 2002 and December 2015. Mean implicit preference for the young was 0.45 with a standard deviation of 0.39, a preference found at every age. Implicit preference for the young was highest among older adults, with age terms of β = .06, β = -.16 and β = .12 for the linear, quadratic and cubic effects, all p < .001. Explicit preference for the young ran the opposite way and was lowest among older adults, β = -.35. Newheiser and Olson tested 117 children aged 7 to 11 after exclusions. White children in majority-White schools scored 0.45, t(52) = 7.59, p < .001, and White children in majority-Black schools 0.35, t(13) = 4.44, p = .001. Black children scored -0.01, t(49) = -0.14, p = .889, while reporting an explicit preference for Black over White at -0.41 in standardised units, p < .01. Among Black children only, explicit preference for rich over poor people predicted an implicit preference for White, β = .35, p = .008, against β = -.14, p = .273, among White children.

study.cite: Axt, J. R., Ebersole, C. R., & Nosek, B. A. (2014). The rules of implicit evaluation by race, religion, and age. Psychological Science, 25(9), 1804-1815.

replicated.unit: MC-IAT D score, children minus old adults, among the 1,020 participants in their sixties

limits: The score is relative, so a value near zero means no preference between the two groups on the day, not warmth toward either. It also hides its own spread. In Jost, Banaji and Nosek's race figure, 39.3% of Black respondents fell in the outgroup-favouring range and 40.1% in the ingroup-favouring one, so the mean of 0.04 describes almost nobody. The race estimate is fragile at that boundary. Nosek, Banaji and Greenwald note in a footnote that restricting the data to unique internet protocol addresses moves the Black respondents' face score to -26 ms, and that the direction switches to a slight preference for Black over White. These samples are volunteers who chose to take a test about bias, and repeat visitors behave differently. Chopik and Giasson report that 37.4% of their respondents had taken a test before, and that the number taken predicted lower implicit preference for the young, β = -.18, p < .001. No standardised effect size for the age reversal was located in a metric comparable to the four-category scores quoted above, which is why no original figure appears in the fields. Rudman, Feinberg and Fairchild's article could not be reached; the server returned 429 to every request across two hours, and the figures attributed to them here are read from Jost, Banaji and Nosek's description rather than from their paper. Jost, Pelham and Carvallo's study of high- and low-status universities is paywalled and is named rather than quoted. Jost and Banaji's 1994 paper was not retrieved. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, PubMed Central, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, OSF and PsyArXiv, Project Implicit's paper archive, and web search.
misreadings: The sign flips between papers reporting the same result. Nosek, Banaji and Greenwald score the race task so that positive means preference for White over Black, giving Black respondents 0.16. Jost, Banaji and Nosek score it so that positive means ingroup favouritism, giving the same respondents -0.16. Two numbers, one finding. The stronger error is to read a mean near zero as a preference for white people. Jost's own sentence is that African Americans showed strong ingroup favouritism explicitly but not implicitly, which is a statement about an absence. On the four-category task the sign goes the other way and Black participants rank their own group first. The claim is domain-specific, and age is where it is solid. Preference for the young survives into the sixties in samples of 49,014 and 704,151, and it is the one case where the authors of the large studies say ingroup favouritism disappears. A third reading treats the pattern as something acquired in adulthood. Newheiser and Olson found the same null in Black seven- to eleven-year-olds, alongside an explicit preference for their own group. A fourth confuses this with the status-legitimacy hypothesis, the survey claim that disadvantaged people rate their society as fairer than advantaged people do. That is a different measure, a different literature and a different verdict, and it has its own entry here.
